name: Dove Grey
lede: Dove grey is the soft plumage color of the dove, and the books disagree on whether it leans blue, pink or purple.

sections.title: One bird, three greys
sections.body:
Paterson defines dove-grey as the bluish grey of the dove's plumage, but his entry for the shorter *dove* describes a pinkish or purplish shade of grey, so one dictionary holds two readings [1]. St Clair's glossary offers a third, a soft, cool-toned mid-grey [2]. Our swatch is the warm reading: ISCC-NBS calls it a "light grayish purplish red", about 5.9 units away, and our earliest record is Maerz and Paul in 1930 [3]. A dove-grey that reads bluer is closer to [[blue-grey]], and a pinker one to [[old-rose]] and [[dusty-rose]] [3].

Paterson also places dove-grey in a long run of animal and weather greys, with oyster, mole, smoke and pearl [1]. Compare [[pearl-grey]] and [[mouse-grey]] [3].

sections.title: In descriptions of paint
sections.body: Ball quotes the art critic Lorenz Dittmann on Millet's *The Gleaners* of 1857, in which the standing figure carries "colourful greys": a silvery blue-grey, dove-grey, and blue and turquoise greys [4]. Ball's point is that words only begin to paint a picture, and dove-grey appears there as one of several grey nuances [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 89 paintings, and in 44 by the stricter within-painting measure [5]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 36 per cent of those works [5].

It peaks in the 1900s, in 1.2 per cent of the 1,674 paintings from that century, about 4.4 times the expected rate, and it is most over-represented in France, at 2.1 times expected [5]. The earliest match is Giorgione's [[painting:commons-Q3937389|panel of about 1503]], which is 427 years before the name's first record, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not a pigment test [5]. Look for it in the grey-mauve of a dove's neck, or in shadowed cloth.
